name: Design a Recommendation System
intent: Choose a few dozen videos out of ten million for each user in under 200 ms, learn from what they watch, and stay useful for brand-new users and brand-new videos.
finalIntro: One home-page request, from candidates to a ranked list, and then the feedback that trains the next model.
prompt: Design the 'recommended for you' feed of a video service with 100 million daily users and 10 million videos. The feed should fit each person's taste, include some variety, give new videos a chance to be seen, work for people who have just signed up, and improve from what people watch.
functional: Return a personalised list of about 20 videos for a user's home page
Show a 'because you watched this' list on a video page
Give a sensible list to a user with no history, and give a new video its first views
Let the business pin, boost or exclude items, such as licensing and age limits
Record what was shown and what was watched, so that the models can learn from it
nonFunctional: A recommendation request answers in under 200 ms at the 99th percentile
Tens of thousands of requests per second at the peak, from a catalogue of ten million videos
A new watch changes the recommendations within minutes, and a new model reaches users daily
A failure in any model or data source degrades the list instead of leaving the page empty
The lists are not all the same and not all one genre, so the catalogue is used widely
Every change to a model is proved by an online experiment before it is shipped to everybody

firstAttempt.text: One SQL table of views: user, video, time. For each request, a query finds the other users who watched the same videos as this user, collects what they watched, counts it, and returns the 20 most common videos that the user has not seen yet.
limits: The query joins huge tables for every page view, so it takes seconds, and tens of thousands of them per second would stop the database
It recommends mostly what is popular, so the lists are alike and the catalogue's long tail is never shown
It has nothing to say about a new user or a new video, which have no rows yet
It cannot weigh watch time, recency, device or time of day, so the order is crude
It records only what was watched, not what was shown, so the system never learns what people ignored

steps.title: Train offline, serve a lookup online
steps.problem: Working out 'people who watched this also watched that' from raw logs takes minutes or hours, and a user cannot wait that long for a page.
steps.fix: Split the system in two. An offline pipeline reads the log of views on a schedule, counts which videos are watched by the same users, and writes the results to a fast key-value store: for each video, its most similar videos, and for each user, a first list. The online API answers a request by reading a few keys, which takes a few milliseconds. The expensive work happens once per batch, not once per request.
steps.tradeoff: Requests become cheap and predictable, and the models can be as heavy as the batch machines allow. The tables are as old as the last batch, so a video watched a minute ago is not yet reflected, and two systems must agree on the format of what is exchanged.

steps.title: Generate candidates from several sources
steps.problem: Scoring all ten million videos for each request is impossible, and one source of suggestions finds only one kind of video.
steps.fix: Stage one is cheap and wide: several generators each propose a few hundred videos, and the union is about 500 candidates. Item-to-item co-occurrence takes the videos the user watched and returns videos often watched by the same people, scored by cosine similarity, meaning co-watches divided by the square root of the two videos' watch counts, so that blockbusters do not win just because everyone watched them. An embedding model places users and videos in one vector space, and an approximate nearest neighbour index, such as a graph or an inverted-file index, returns the closest videos to the user's vector in a few milliseconds without comparing against all ten million. Popular and trending lists fill the gaps.
steps.tradeoff: Ten million videos become 500 in a few milliseconds, and the sources cover each other's blind spots. The approximate index can miss a true neighbour, the candidates lock in what the generators can find, and a video that no generator proposes can never be recommended, however good the ranker is.

steps.title: Rank the candidates with a model and a feature store
steps.problem: Candidates come from different sources with scores that cannot be compared, and 'similar' is not the same as 'this user will watch it now'.
steps.fix: A ranking model, typically gradient-boosted trees or a neural network, predicts for each of the 500 candidates the chance of a click and the expected watch time, from features of the user (recent watches, device, hour of the day), of the video (age, genre, quality) and of the pair. The features are read from a feature store: a low-latency online copy for serving and a historical copy for training, both filled by the same definitions. That keeps training and serving consistent, and it avoids the classic bug where a feature is computed one way in training and another way in production. Scoring 500 candidates takes tens of milliseconds.
steps.tradeoff: The order reflects many signals, and the objective can be tuned toward watch time rather than raw clicks. The model is a new dependency to run and keep fresh, features can be stale or missing and need defaults, and a mismatch between the training and serving data silently makes the model worse.

steps.title: Re-rank for variety and business rules
steps.problem: A model that always maximises the chance of a click fills the list with near-duplicates of one genre, and it knows nothing about licensing, age limits or promotions.
steps.fix: A final, cheap stage takes the ranked list and builds the page. It filters out what the user has already watched and what must not be shown to them, applies pins and exclusions from the business, and then picks greedily for diversity: each time it takes the video with the best adjusted score, where the score is divided by one plus the number of videos of that genre already chosen, a simple form of maximal marginal relevance. It also caps how many videos come from one channel. Rules sit outside the model, so changing a rule needs no retraining.
steps.tradeoff: Lists are varied, and the business can steer them at once. A little of the predicted engagement is traded for variety, so the hit rate on held-out watches falls by a few points, and the long-run benefit has to be shown in an experiment rather than assumed.

steps.title: Handle new users and new videos
steps.problem: Co-occurrence and embeddings need history. A new user has none, and a new video has no watches, so the generators can never propose it.
steps.fix: For a new user, fall back to what needs no history: the popular and trending videos in their country and language, then what they said when signing up, then quickly adapt as soon as they have watched a few videos, since a handful of watches already allows item-to-item lookups. For a new video, use its content: genre, title, creator and a content embedding, which can place it near similar videos before anyone has watched it. Reserve an exploration slot in some lists to show the new video to a small sample of users, so that it gets its first real watches, and let the data decide from there.
steps.tradeoff: Nobody gets an empty page, and the catalogue does not freeze around what is already popular. Exploration costs a slot that could have held a safer choice, and a poor video wastes some views before the data shows it is poor.

steps.title: Close the loop: log everything, and test every change
steps.problem: Without logs of what was shown, the system cannot learn what users ignored, and without experiments nobody knows whether a new model is actually better.
steps.fix: The API writes an event for every impression (what was shown, in what position, by which model version) and every click and watch, to an event log. The offline pipeline reads it to build training data, so the loop is closed: recommendations create the data that trains the next recommendations. Every change goes through an A/B experiment: users are assigned to groups by a hash of the user id, and groups are compared on click-through rate, watch time and retention over days, with a guardrail on latency and on catalogue coverage. Offline numbers such as hit rate or precision at k on held-out watches are used to choose what is worth testing, not to decide what ships.
steps.tradeoff: The system improves with use, and a bad model is caught before everybody sees it. The log is large, because impressions outnumber clicks about ten to one, a model trained only on what it showed learns its own bias and keeps popular videos popular, and experiments need enough traffic and enough days to give a reliable answer.

failures.scenario: The ranking model or the feature store is slow or down
failures.impact: Every request waits for the ranker, and the home page times out for everyone.
failures.answer: Give the ranker a tight timeout and a circuit breaker. If it fails, serve the candidates ordered by their generator scores, or a precomputed per-segment popular list, and mark the response as degraded. A missing feature is replaced by a default, so one source being down costs quality, not availability.

failures.scenario: A bad model is shipped, or the training data was broken
failures.impact: Recommendations quietly get worse for millions of users, and nothing crashes to tell anyone.
failures.answer: New models first run on a small share of traffic in an experiment, with guardrail metrics on watch time, click-through rate and coverage, and alerts if they drop. Each model has a version that is logged with every impression, and the previous model stays deployed so that a rollback is a flag change. Training data is checked for sudden changes in size and distribution before a model is built.

failures.scenario: The feedback loop narrows what is shown
failures.impact: Videos that were shown get watched, so they are shown more, while the rest of the catalogue gets no views and the feed gets samey.
failures.answer: Log the exposure, so the model can correct for position and for what it chose not to show. Keep exploration slots, diversity in the re-ranker and a coverage guardrail in every experiment. Train on a sample that includes randomised or less personalised lists, so the model sees what users do when the model did not pick for them.

failures.scenario: Events are lost or duplicated on the way to the training data
failures.impact: Clicks are missing or counted twice, so labels are wrong and the model learns from a distorted picture.
failures.answer: Events carry a unique id, the log keeps them durable, and the pipeline de-duplicates on the id. An impression is joined with the click that follows it, within a window. Counts of events per hour are monitored, so a drop is noticed in hours, not weeks.

alternatives.title: How to propose candidates

options.name: Popularity only
options.pro: Trivial, always available, and good for new users
options.con: The same list for everybody, and the rest of the catalogue is never shown

options.name: Item-to-item co-occurrence
options.pro: Simple, explainable ('because you watched X'), and strong with little machinery
options.con: Needs watches on both videos, and tends to stay close to what the user already likes

options.name: Embeddings with approximate nearest neighbour search
options.pro: Captures taste that co-watching misses, and can use content for new items
options.con: A model and an index to train and run, with a small chance of missing the true nearest

alternatives.pick: Use several: popularity as the fallback, item-to-item as the workhorse, embeddings for reach, and merge their candidates.

alternatives.title: When recommendations are computed

options.name: Batch, precomputed per user
options.pro: Very cheap to serve, and heavy models are affordable
options.con: Stale, and wasted for users who never come back

options.name: Online, at request time
options.pro: Uses the latest context, such as what was watched a minute ago
options.con: Latency budget and serving cost on every request

options.name: Batch for candidates, online for ranking
options.pro: Heavy work is done in advance, and the last step uses fresh context

alternatives.pick: Batch the embeddings and the similarity tables, and rank online with fresh features.

alternatives.title: What the ranker optimises

options.name: Click-through rate
options.pro: Plentiful labels, and easy to measure

options.name: A blend with long-term signals
options.pro: Balances clicks, watching, and whether users come back
options.con: Weights must be tuned, and can only be judged in long experiments

alternatives.pick: A weighted blend of the click and the watch-time predictions, with retention as the metric that decides experiments.

alternatives.title: How to judge a change

options.name: Offline metrics on held-out data
options.pro: Fast, cheap and repeatable, so many ideas can be screened
options.con: Biased by what the old system showed, and not the same as user value

options.name: Online A/B test
options.pro: Measures real behaviour, including effects the offline data cannot see
options.con: Needs traffic and days, and every test exposes some users to a risk

alternatives.pick: Screen with offline hit rate and precision at k, then decide with an online experiment and guardrails.

quiz.question: The home page query joins a billion-row views table to find users who watched the same videos. It takes about 3 seconds, and traffic peaks at 30,000 requests per second. What is the right change?
options: Add composite indexes on user and video in the views table, so the join runs on index lookups instead of full scans of the table.
Add 30 read replicas of the database and spread the requests across them, so each handles about 1,000 queries per second.
Cache each user's finished list for an hour, so repeat visits skip the query, while first visits and new users still run the full join.
Compute video similarity offline on a schedule and keep each video's top similar videos in a key-value store.
quiz.explanation: The expensive work should happen once per batch, not once per page view, and the API then reads a few keys in milliseconds. Indexes and replicas still run a heavy join 30,000 times per second, which is about 90,000 queries in flight at 3 seconds each. A per-user cache misses for most of 100 million users and cannot serve new ones.

quiz.question: A user watched video A (10,000 watchers in total). Candidate B has 8,000 watchers, 4,000 of whom also watched A. Candidate X is a blockbuster with 4,000,000 watchers, 5,000 of whom also watched A. The generator should suggest the video with the stronger link to A. Which scoring does that?
options: Raw co-watch count: X scores 5,000 and B 4,000, so X ranks first, as more shared viewers mean a stronger link between the videos.
Co-watches divided by A's watch count only: X scores 0.50 and B 0.40, which cancels the effect of A's own popularity on every candidate's score.
Co-watches divided by the square root of the product of the two watch counts: B scores about 0.45 and X about 0.025, so B ranks first.
Raw co-watch count multiplied by the log of the candidate's watch count, to favour videos with proven appeal.
quiz.explanation: Almost everyone watched the blockbuster, so its overlap with A says little. Dividing by the square root of both counts compares the overlap with what chance would give. Dividing by A's count alone still ranks X first, because it ignores how popular the candidate is, and the other two options push blockbusters up even more.

quiz.question: A team trains the ranker only on clicks from lists the ranker itself chose. After six months, 5% of the catalogue gets 80% of the views and new videos barely appear. Offline hit rate on held-out watches still looks fine. What is the best response?
options: Log every impression with its position and model version, keep exploration slots and some less personalised traffic in the training data.
Retrain the ranker hourly instead of daily, so it picks up new watches faster and new videos get data sooner than before, with far less lag.
Switch to a bigger neural ranker that optimises click-through harder, since better predictions will find the long tail of the catalogue by themselves.
Add a fixed score bonus for videos younger than seven days for every user, so that new videos always surface in the lists they see.
quiz.explanation: The model only learns from what it chose to show, so popular videos stay popular. Logging exposure, exploring, and guarding coverage break that loop and let experiments see the harm that offline hit rate hides. Faster retraining and a bigger model learn the same bias sooner, and a blanket bonus wastes views without measuring anything.
